extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral and political philosophy; readers studying Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and organizes Aristotle's evaluative claims about the nature of happiness, the requirements of virtue, the role of external goods, and the formation of political/legislative skill as presented in Book X (with editorial notes). Useful for analyzing standards for a 'good life' and for statesmanship in Aristotelian terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as contemplative activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is co-extensive with Contemplative Speculation; the perfect Happiness must be a kind of Contemplative Working (the exercise of the highest faculty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that the gods' life is contemplative and therefore their blessed activity is speculation; human happiness is highest in proportion as one partakes in that contemplative activity. Animals lack this and so cannot be happy. (See: 'Happiness then is co-extensive with this Contemplative Speculation.')

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods are necessary but limited for human contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although contemplation is supreme, man (unlike gods) requires external prosperity — health, nourishment, bodily well-being, and other external goods — to enable speculative life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External goods are instruments for action and speculation but need not be many or great; moderate means can suffice for noble action. Examples: Solon's picture of the happy (moderately supplied), Anaxagoras' remark that the happy may seem strange to the multitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue requires both moral choice and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral choice and actions both contribute to Virtue; perfection of virtuous action requires both choice and the relevant actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle raises the question whether moral choice or actions weigh more in Virtue, concluding both are required, and that actions often require many additional things (external conditions) to be performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different virtues demand different external means
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific virtues presuppose particular external capacities: the liberal man needs money, the just man needs resources to meet obligations, the brave man needs power/opportunity, the self-mastered need temptation to display mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that the possibility of virtuous action depends on appropriate external conditions — without them the relevant virtue cannot be exercised or displayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplative life best approximates divine blessedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions characteristic of moral virtues (justice, liberality, bravery) would be trivial or absurd if attributed to gods; by contrast the gods' working is contemplative, so contemplation is nearest the divine and most fitting for highest human happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses the implausibility of picturing gods engaged in ordinary moral transactions to motivate contemplation as the highest human good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and activity: happiness is activity, not passive possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is a form of working (activity), specifically contemplative activity, and not mere possession or passive state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle stresses action/working as constitutive of happiness; if from a living being you take away action, what remains is contemplation, reinforcing activity's centrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of virtuous character depends on nature, custom, and teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Becoming good is attributed variously to Nature, Custom, and Teaching; Nature may be beyond our control, but custom (habituation) and teaching are crucial for moral formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and precept alone are often insufficient; there must be a prior disposition (soil) to receive instruction. Habituation (early training in food, manners, living) readies the mind to accept moral principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early education and habituation should be legally regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: Food, manner of living, and upbringing in youth ought to be subjects of legal regulation because habits formed early become ingrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle cites Sparta (Lacedaemonian) as an example of attention to these points and argues that public systems should ideally shape youths' habits, otherwise individuals must take responsibility for training their own children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of honor, punishment, and expulsion to shape moral behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawgivers should employ the sense of honour to exhort well-trained citizens, impose chastisement and penalties on those less promising, and expel the incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The good, guided by honour, will obey reason; the baser sort respond to compulsion and punishment. Pains should be counter to the pleasures they seek.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law's authority surpasses paternal rule for public moral formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Paternal rule lacks compulsion; the law, as a declaration from Practical Wisdom and Intellect, has coercive power and is less a target of hatred even when enforcing right rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for public legal regulation (rather than mere paternal command) as more effective for shaping conduct across a community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private care can better attend individual cases than public systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Private training has advantages in treating particular cases because individual differences can be attended to more exactly than by generalized public rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: medicine (a fever case may need private judgement), boxing (different opponents need different methods). But private care should still be informed by general principles/science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science/theory plus practice are both necessary for true statesmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Political skill (legislation/statesmanship) requires not only familiarity with laws and constitutions but also practical experience; practice contributes materially and theoretical knowledge alone (or merely collecting laws) is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophists purported to teach statesmanship but often neither practiced it nor produced statesmen; compilations of laws alone do not create legislatures any more than medical compilations alone make physicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collections of laws are useful only to qualified judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilations of laws and constitutions help those capable of speculative judgement and of understanding relations among elements, but they will not enable unqualified persons to choose or legislate rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to medical and artistic treatises: treatises aid professionals but not the unlearned; similarly collections of laws aid those with practical/theoretical qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuals must become 'legislators of themselves' when public systems fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Where public systems neglect upbringing, individuals should aim to 'make a Legislator of himself' — i.e., take personal responsibility for training children and friends in virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical recommendation when ideal public regulation is absent; good laws are those formed by practical wisdom and used in training individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political science should be investigated empirically and comparatively
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine what constitutions and regulations are best, one should collect fragments of predecessors' statements and examine polities to ascertain what preserves or destroys communities and particular constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rubric: study existing constitutions, analyze causes of success/failure, and then form conclusions about the best regulations for each case.
